analysis.one_liner: Removes the $75 million cap on oil companies' liability for offshore oil spills.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was introduced in July 2016, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, a company responsible for an offshore oil spill pays all cleanup costs plus damages capped at $75 million beyond cleanup. This bill would remove that $75 million cap, making the polluter liable for the full cost of the damage — lost natural resources, lost property and business income, and the extra public services (like fire protection) a spill forces communities to provide [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism businesses, and taxpayers. If a major spill happens, the companies responsible — not the public — would pay the full cost of damaged natural resources, lost livelihoods, and emergency services [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million cap on a responsible party's liability for damages from an offshore oil discharge, beyond removal costs [S2][S3].

Makes responsible parties liable for damages including loss of natural resources, property, revenue, or profits, and the costs of public services like fire protection during and after cleanup [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face potentially unlimited liability for the full damages of any spill they cause, and their insurers and investors, who bear higher and less predictable spill risk [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil companies and their insurers

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability creates unpredictable and potentially catastrophic financial exposure for offshore drillers, which critics argue could push smaller operators out of deepwater drilling and could raise insurance costs and energy prices [S3].
The bill does not change the underlying spill-prevention rules or add any new safety requirements; it only changes who pays after a disaster [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is that the public would no longer absorb the cost of a catastrophic spill once damages exceed the current $75 million cap — a cap set in 1990 that a Deepwater Horizon-scale disaster can exceed billions of times over. The cost falls on the companies whose drilling creates the risk, through higher liability, insurance, and compliance costs that could partly show up in energy prices. The strongest honest objection is the unpredictability of unlimited liability, which is precisely why the cap was set in 1990; the bill's answer is that the party causing the damage, not the public, should bear it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 12, 2016, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez (D-NJ) introduced the bill on July 12, 2016, with 10 Democratic cosponsors, roughly two and a half months after the sixth anniversary of the Deepwater Horizon spill [S1][S3][S4].
The bill's only action beyond introduction was its referral to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee never held a markup, reported the bill out, or scheduled a floor vote, and the bill received no further action before the Congress ended [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies keep the current $75 million liability cap, so the public continues to absorb spill damages beyond that amount. Nothing in the provided record shows a committee hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies and their insurers

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it died in a committee without any recorded votes [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would end their $75 million liability cap and make them pay all damages from spills they cause, potentially billions of dollars for a Deepwater Horizon-scale event. Their interest in keeping the cap runs directly against the public interest in having polluters pay for the damage [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Coastal fishing, seafood, and tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses bear the losses of a spill — closed fisheries, cancelled trips, damaged reputations — and currently can be shortchanged once the $75 million cap is hit. Unlimited liability makes the polluter cover their full losses [S2][S3].
Unlimited liability makes spill risk far harder to price and cap, raising premiums for offshore coverage and shrinking what insurers will underwrite [S3].
